nameStory: The rabbit tick gets its straightforward name from its favorite dining companions - rabbits and hares! These tiny hitchhikers have formed such a close relationship with cottontails and their cousins that they're rarely found anywhere else. It's occasionally called the grouse tick when it decides to sample some feathered friends instead.
description: The rabbit tick is a small, reddish-brown hard tick that's perfectly designed for life on furry hosts. Like other hard ticks, it has a tough, shield-like plate called a scutum that gives it a shiny, armored appearance. Its mouthparts project forward prominently from its teardrop-shaped body, and many people say it looks just like a miniature version of the common wood tick. These specialized parasites are rarely seen by people since they prefer to stay hidden in rabbit fur.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Teardrop-shaped body with a hard, shiny shield (scutum) that feels smooth and rigid to the touch, like a tiny plastic bead

idTips.label: Capitulum
idTips.description: Mouthparts project forward prominently from the body like a small beak - this forward-pointing capitulum is very noticeable when viewed from above

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Reddish-brown to dark brown coloration with the scutum often appearing glossy and darker than the rest of the body

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small tick that's easily overlooked - unfed adults are quite tiny and feel like a small, firm seed when handled

idTips.label: Host Association
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on rabbits, hares, and occasionally ground-feeding birds - rarely encountered crawling freely

habitat: Look for rabbit ticks wherever cottontails and other rabbits make their homes - brushy areas, field edges, woodland clearings, and suburban areas with dense shrubs. They thrive in the ground-level microhabitats where rabbits feed and nest, including areas with thick grass, brambles, and low vegetation. You're most likely to encounter them if you're handling rabbits or in areas with high rabbit populations.

seasonality.spring: Adult ticks become active as temperatures warm, seeking rabbit hosts for blood meals. This is when you're most likely to find engorged females preparing to lay eggs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with all life stages present. Larvae and nymphs are actively seeking their first and second blood meals on young rabbits and other small mammals.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding and mating on hosts. Late fall activity depends on temperature, with ticks becoming less active as cold weather approaches.
seasonality.winter: Generally inactive in harsh New England winters, overwintering in protected locations in leaf litter or soil near rabbit habitats.

funFact: This tiny tick has achieved one of the most impressive travel records in the arachnid world - its range stretches from Alaska all the way to Argentina, making it one of the most widely distributed ticks native to the Americas!
confusionNotes: Rabbit ticks are often confused with young deer ticks or dog ticks, but remember the "rabbit rule" - if you didn't find it on or near a rabbit, it's probably not a rabbit tick! The prominent forward-projecting mouthparts also help distinguish it from other small ticks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "rabbit tick," these arachnids occasionally earn the alternate name "grouse tick" when they're found on ground-feeding birds. This dual naming can cause confusion, but it's the same species adapting to different available hosts in the same low-to-ground habitat.
compareHints: The rabbit tick differs from its relative, the Asian longhorned tick, primarily in its host preferences and native range - while rabbit ticks are New World natives specializing in rabbits, Asian longhorned ticks are recent arrivals that prefer larger mammals like deer and livestock. The rabbit tick's strong association with lagomorphs (rabbits and hares) makes it much more specialized than most other hard ticks in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative the rabbit tick (the only other Haemaphysalis species in New England), the Asian longhorned tick is more likely to be found on larger mammals and domestic animals rather than primarily on rabbits.
